title: Not even Zeus
hook: "I'll chain your leg." "My leg, yes; my will, not even Zeus can conquer" (Discourses 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: grammar, gold, and Zeus explaining his one gift, the right use of impressions. Your line was the gift of use.

A tyrant leans across the table and lists what he can do to you. Chains. Prison. Worse. Epictetus stages this scene in the first discourse as a quick back-and-forth, almost like a comedy sketch. He wasn't writing from the safe side of power. He grew up enslaved, with no say over his own body, and that gives his answers a particular weight. Notice who gets the funny lines. It isn't the man with the chains.
screen: `A TYRANT LISTS WHAT HE CAN DO.` → `CHAINS. PRISON. WORSE.` → `NOT EVEN ZEUS.`

segments.voice: Later in the first discourse, Epictetus runs through the hard things. I must die. Must I die groaning too? I must be chained. Must I also whine about it? I must be exiled. Does anyone stop me from going with a smile, cheerful and calm? Then the scene. Tell me your secrets, says the tyrant. I won't; that's up to me. Then I'll chain you. What are you saying, man? You'll chain my leg. My will, not even Zeus can overpower. I'll throw you in prison. You mean my little body. I'll cut off your head. Well, when did I ever tell you mine was the only neck in the world that couldn't be cut? The will he means is prohairesis, the power to choose, to judge, to assent or refuse. In the Discourses it names the part of you that's truly yours. A tyrant can move your body anywhere. He can't make you agree that his threat is your harm. Later writers told a story that Epictetus' master once twisted his leg, and Epictetus calmly warned, you'll break it. When it broke, he said: didn't I tell you? Nobody knows if that happened, and another ancient source says he was simply lame from illness. But the Discourses never ask anyone to pretend chains don't hurt. They ask a narrower question: inside this constraint, what is still yours? These, Epictetus says, are the things to rehearse, to write down every day, to practice. Not because a tyrant is coming. Because small chains come every week.
screen: `MUST I DIE GROANING TOO?` · `MY LEG, YES. MY WILL, NOT EVEN ZEUS.` · `PROHAIRESIS: THE POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `INSIDE THE CONSTRAINT, WHAT'S YOURS?` · then, large: `NOT EVEN ZEUS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one constraint you're living inside right now, a job you can't leave yet, an illness, a tight budget, a body that won't do what it used to, and name it plainly. Then ask Epictetus' question: inside this, what is still mine? How I speak, what I notice, what I agree to, where I put my attention: find one, and rest there.
Prohairesis. The power to choose, to judge, to assent or refuse; chain the leg, but not even Zeus can overpower it. Today's word.
Your line: what is still yours. The leg can be chained; the will can't. Day three hundred ninety, done.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often rehearse hard situations in advance and ask, inside each constraint, what still belongs to them: their choices, judgments and attention.

chat.meaning: In Discourses one, chapter one, a tyrant can chain the leg, but not even Zeus can overpower the will, prohairesis.

prohairesis.meaning: the power to choose, judge, assent or refuse

Zeus.meaning: the chief Greek god; even he can't overpower the will

Discourses.meaning: Arrian's record of Epictetus teaching in class

Epictetus.meaning: a Stoic teacher who grew up enslaved

sources.ref: Origen, Against Celsus 7.53 (the leg story); Simplicius, Commentary on the Enchiridion (lameness)

notes: Discourses 1.1 paraphrased: 'I must die: must I die lamenting? be fettered: lamenting too? exiled: does anyone hinder me from going with a smile?'; the tyrant dialogue: secrets, chains ('my leg you will fetter, but my will not even Zeus can overpower'), prison ('my body'), beheading ('when did I tell you that I alone had a neck that cannot be severed?'); these things philosophers should rehearse and write daily. Confirm sections; Long 1877 could be quoted if verified.
The broken-leg story is from Celsus as reported by Origen, Contra Celsum 7.53; Simplicius and the Suda attribute lameness to illness/rheumatism. Presented as uncertain. Confirm.
Greek προαίρεσις: confirm it is the word in 1.1 for 'will'.
